title: Tarte Tatin
subtitle: Upside-down caramelised apple tart
excerpt: The great French upside-down tart: apples cooked in butter and caramel directly in the baking tin, covered with pastry and baked until the pastry is crisp, then inverted onto a plate. The apples come out glazed, yielding, and deeply caramelised.

recipe.sourceNotes: Tarte Tatin is named after Stéphanie and Caroline Tatin, who ran the Hôtel Tatin in Lamotte-Beuvron in the Loire Valley, France. The story goes that Stéphanie accidentally cooked the apples in butter and sugar before putting the pastry on, then inverted the tart to rescue it; this is probably a romanticised retelling, but the dish itself dates from the late nineteenth century. It was championed by the Maxim's restaurant in Paris, which added it to their menu in the early twentieth century and spread its fame internationally. The technique requires caramelising the apples on the hob before the pastry goes on top, then inverting the finished tart. The timing of the inversion is the only tricky step: too soon and the caramel runs everywhere; too late and the tart sticks.

content.text: Use a heavy ovenproof frying pan or a dedicated tarte tatin tin; the pan goes from hob to oven. Cook the caramel until it is deep amber, not golden: pale caramel tastes sweet and flat; deep caramel has bitterness that balances the apples. Invert the tart while still warm but not just out of the oven; leave it to cool for 5 minutes first so the caramel begins to set slightly.

items.preparation: Cox or Braeburn; peeled, cored, and quartered

content.text: Heat the oven to 200°C / fan 180°C / gas 6. Peel, core, and quarter the apples. In a 24 cm ovenproof frying pan, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the sugar and cook without stirring until a deep amber caramel forms, about 8 minutes. Watch it carefully.

Remove from the heat. Add the vanilla and arrange the apple quarters tightly in the caramel, standing them on their edges in concentric circles. Return to the heat and cook for 5 minutes until the apples have softened slightly and absorbed some caramel.

Lay a circle of rolled shortcrust or puff pastry over the apples, tucking the edges down around the inside of the pan. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until the pastry is golden and crisp. Remove from the oven and leave to cool for 5 minutes. Place a plate larger than the pan over it and invert confidently in one motion. Serve warm with crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream.
